summary: Graphical, command-line, natural-language and gesture-recognition user interfaces — how they work, who they suit, and their advantages and disadvantages.

blocks.content: An interface in which the user interacts with the computer through **graphical elements** — windows, icons, menus and a pointer (**WIMP**) — usually with a mouse or touchscreen.

rows: Easy to learn and use; no commands to remember
Uses more memory, processing power and storage
Suitable for beginners and non-technical users
Slower for experienced users doing repetitive tasks
Many clicks/menus may be needed for one action
WYSIWYG — see the result while editing

blocks.content: An interface in which the user types **text commands** at a prompt, and the computer replies with text.

C:\Users\student> mkdir Project
C:\Users\student> cd Project
C:\Users\student\Project> copy ..\report.docx .
        1 file(s) copied.
blocks.caption: Example CLI session (Windows)

rows: Fast for experienced users — one command can do a lot
Difficult to learn; commands and syntax must be remembered
Needs very little memory and processing power
Typing errors cause commands to fail
Commands can be combined into scripts to **automate** tasks
Gives full, precise control of the system
No visual feedback; easy to make a destructive mistake
Useful for remote administration of servers

blocks.title: GUI vs CLI
rows: Few typing errors, but slower navigation

blocks.content: A comparison answer needs **both sides** in each point: "A GUI is **easier to learn** than a CLI **because** the user does not need to remember commands."
The user communicates in **everyday human language**, spoken or typed, and the computer interprets the meaning. *Examples: Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant, chatbots.*

blocks.title: Natural language interface
rows: Very natural — no special training needed
Accents, dialects and background noise cause misunderstanding
Hands-free — useful while driving or for people with disabilities
Language is ambiguous; the system may misinterpret the request
Privacy concerns — devices may record conversations
Limited vocabulary and languages; needs internet and processing power

blocks.content: The computer recognises **movements of the body** (hands, fingers, head, eyes) using cameras, touchscreens or sensors and turns them into commands. *Examples: swiping on a phone, Microsoft Kinect, VR controllers, smart TV hand gestures.*

blocks.title: Gesture recognition interface
rows: Intuitive and natural; no keyboard or mouse
Gestures may be misread or performed accidentally
Good for games, VR and accessibility
A limited set of gestures; users must learn them

blocks.title: Choosing an interface
blocks.content:
- A surgeon viewing X-rays during an operation → **gesture recognition** (hands are sterile, no touching).
- A network administrator configuring 50 servers → **CLI** (scripts automate the work).
- A child using a learning app → **GUI** (easy, visual).
- A driver who wants directions → **natural language** (hands-free).
